title: How to Read Cannabis Plant Science Critically
objective: Distinguish observation, mechanism, controlled evidence, practical guidance, and legal requirements before accepting a cultivation claim.

terms.definition: A report of an original experiment or observation with described methods and data.
Applying a result beyond the tested genotype, environment, stage, or production system.
A factor that changes with the tested factor and could explain the observed result.
A practical value used to begin monitoring; not a universal biological optimum.

coreScience: Cannabis information is unusually vulnerable to overstatement. Decades of legal restriction limited formal crop research while an experienced but largely informal grower culture developed its own vocabulary, target ranges, and cause-and-effect explanations. Both sources can contain useful observations. Neither should be accepted without asking what was measured, how it was measured, what plants were tested, and what alternative explanation could fit the result.

A strong claim identifies the genetic material, developmental stage, root-zone system, environmental conditions, treatment, sample size, measurement method, and uncertainty. A weak claim uses a cultivar name as if it were a verified genetic identity, changes several inputs at once, reports only the best plant, or treats a visual impression as proof of a biochemical change. Yield, cannabinoid concentration, terpene composition, disease response, and morphology are all affected by genotype and environment; a result from one crop cannot automatically become a rule for all cannabis.

Evidence also has different jobs. Primary cannabis research is best for cannabis-specific response. Hemp extension literature is often practical and valuable, but fiber, grain, and cannabinoid hemp can differ from indoor drug-type flower production. General horticulture explains mechanisms such as water potential, nutrient availability, and disease cycles, but those sources should be labeled as general plant science. Regulations, pesticide labels, equipment manuals, and laboratory standards answer different questions and can override a general recommendation in their own domain.
cultivationRelevance: Before changing a crop, write the hypothesis in plain language: what is wrong, what evidence supports that diagnosis, what single change is proposed, and what measurement will show whether it worked. This converts reaction into controlled learning.

Numerical targets require context. A temperature, VPD, PPFD, DLI, pH, EC, or drying value should be described as a study condition, measured response, practical starting range, equipment limit, or legal limit. Calling every number an optimum creates false precision.

Use an evidence ladder when deciding whether to change a crop: first define the observation, then identify plausible mechanisms, then check cannabis-specific studies where available, then use general plant science to test whether the mechanism is biologically coherent, and finally compare the claim against your own repeatable records. A recommendation becomes stronger when independent evidence types point in the same direction and weaker when it depends on one uncontrolled observation.

Treat every intervention as a small experiment whenever practical. Keep unaffected comparison plants or previous-cycle baselines, change as few variables as possible, define the expected response before acting, and set a review time. This reduces hindsight bias and helps separate true improvement from normal plant-to-plant variation, environmental drift, measurement error, or regression toward the mean.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Write the exact claim in testable language, the crop decision it would change, and whether it is being treated as established evidence, a practical starting range, a manufacturer instruction, a regulatory requirement, or a hypothesis that still needs testing.

Record citation, source type, publication date, whether the work directly studied cannabis/hemp or another crop, peer-review or regulatory status, and any obvious conflict-of-interest or vendor context. Preserve the original wording of important limitations.

Record genotype or accession, propagation type, developmental stage, plant age, root-zone system, environment, treatment duration, sample size, control group, and which plant tissue or response variable was evaluated. Mark any context that does not match the crop you are managing.

Record the variable, instrument or laboratory method, units, calibration or quality-control information when available, sampling location, sampling time, replicate structure, uncertainty, and whether the reported difference was biological, statistical, or only visual.

List at least one plausible confounder or alternative mechanism. Note what observation or measurement would weaken each explanation. Do not label a diagnosis confirmed when the evidence only establishes correlation or a symptom pattern.

Record whether the claim is accepted for the current context, rejected, or retained as a hypothesis; what action was taken; what comparison or baseline will be used; when the result will be reviewed; and whether repeated cycles support the same conclusion.

misconceptions: Published means proven: Publication quality varies, and one study rarely establishes a universal cultivation rule.
Anecdotes are worthless: Repeated observations can generate strong hypotheses; they are not the same as controlled evidence.
One perfect target exists: The useful target depends on plant response, genotype, stage, measurement method, and management goal.
evidenceLimits: Evidence hierarchies help organize questions but do not remove the need to inspect methods. A peer-reviewed paper can still have weak controls or narrow applicability, while a repeated grower observation can be valuable for hypothesis generation without proving mechanism. Cannabis-specific evidence remains uneven across genetics, environments, production systems, and postharvest practices; general horticulture can explain mechanisms but should be labeled when cannabis was not studied. Numerical targets should therefore carry their source, context, measurement method, and uncertainty rather than being presented as universal optima.
